title: Draft: Qt: Add FlowLayout and use it in the search frame
description:
Add Qt's example FlowLayout, and use it in the search frame to
switch the number of rows depending on the width of the window.

In AccordionFrame, make sure to update the maximum height (set
from the animation) when the height needed for a particular width
changes.

notes.body: Still a WIP, as I would rearrange the buttons and also try to center things vertically (which Qt's default FlowLayout doesn't do, assuming all the same widget). It has the basic idea (and could be used for the other temporary toolbars.)

I do not think to copy the whole example verbatim 1:1 is a good idea. I get the concept, but in this case I think it might introduce more issues than it is worth. Especially in the license game, as it introduces code with a different license, I'd prefer the code stays our own. 

Don't get me wrong, taking the idea and using it is a great thing, I just have issue with the 1:1 copy.
Btw, we are a desktop application. A FlowLayout is more common to a web or mobile application. I think this is the wrong direction to go for this issue.

Yeah, this was partially as a proof of concept, and we would have to change it. I'm not completely sure if it's the right approach, but I do understand the complaint that the toolbar looks kind of odd when the resolution is wide enough that it could fit comfortably on one row, but it's too big to make it one row on narrower resolutions.

The license isn't too bad, because they license it under the BSD-3-Clause, and we already have a fair amount of code with that license.

Still, the license issue aside (and as mentioned before I do not really care but think it should be avoided), it breaks UX concepts.

We should avoid striving too far from UX concepts as it may make integration with platforms more difficult. Apple for instance has a history to force certain items on an application which we had to actively remove. The toolbar might seem inconspicuous for that, but I would not put it past that. Also, users tend to combine expectations of app behavior. So if one part of the app behaves like a mobile/web application, they expect other parts to do so as well. That will lead to adoption issues.

In the past for instance, we had a change that would have put Wireshark in a full-screen mode like a kiosk mode. It is a great idea, but not for an application. Because users will not understand how to return. Therefore I would avoid changes that strive too far from an expected app behavior.

Yes, part of the problem is that UI that looks fine with fusion or with any Windows or Linux other style that I've tried looks bad with the default macOS style, and I don't have a Mac to really test any fixes. I should just let someone who does make the search frame toolbar look better on Mac, I guess, rather than try to fix it blind.
